pages.x: In 1862 King Wilhelm I of Prussia made Otto von Bismarck his chief minister. In his first big speech Bismarck said that the great questions of the day would be settled not by speeches and majority votes, the mistake of 1848, but by iron and blood. He meant to unite Germany under Prussia, and to push Austria out.

First, in 1864, Prussia and Austria together took the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark. The British statesman Palmerston joked that only three people had ever understood the Schleswig-Holstein question: one was dead, one had gone mad, and he himself had forgotten it.

Two years later Bismarck picked a quarrel with Austria over the duchies. Prussia's railways rushed its armies to the front, and its soldiers' breech-loading needle guns fired far faster than the Austrians' rifles. At Königgrätz in Bohemia in July 1866 Austria was crushed in a day. The whole war took seven weeks.

Prussia swallowed Hanover and the other northern states that had sided with Austria, and bound the rest of the north into a new union under its king. Austria was shut out of Germany for good. Only the Catholic south, Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden, stayed apart.

In 1870 France protested at a German prince being offered the throne of Spain. The French ambassador met King Wilhelm at the spa town of Ems and asked him to promise it would never happen again. Bismarck cut the king's telegram about the meeting so that it read like a snub, and gave it to the press. France, as he had hoped, declared war.

The southern states joined Prussia, and the German armies, faster and better led, poured into France. On 2 September 1870, at Sedan, a French army of over 100,000 men surrendered, and with it Emperor Napoleon III himself. Paris declared a republic and was besieged all winter.

During the siege of Paris, balloons floated letters and people out over the German lines, and pigeons flew the answers back. As food ran out, Parisians ate horses, cats and rats, and even the two elephants of the zoo, Castor and Pollux.

On 18 January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the palace of the French kings, the German princes proclaimed Wilhelm German Emperor. France had to pay a huge sum and give up Alsace and much of Lorraine, a loss it never forgot.

The new German Empire, with its industry, science and army, was soon the strongest power in Europe. But it was born in war, and France's longing to win back its lost provinces, and the fear Germany's strength stirred in its neighbours, helped lead to the First World War.
pts: Bismarck united Germany by blood and iron
The empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871
